title: Breaking things on purpose
teaches: Timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, retry storms, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding, and Chaos Monkey

blocks.text: In August 2008 Netflix still made most of its money mailing DVDs, and a corruption in one of its main databases stopped it shipping them for three days. The company drew a lesson that shaped the next seven years. A single big database in its own datacentre was a single point of failure, and the way out was to move to Amazon Web Services and build every service on the assumption that any machine it ran on could disappear at any moment. The move took until January 2016.[^migration]

Assuming failure is easy to write in a design document and hard to make true, because the code that handles failure is the code that never runs. So in 2010 Netflix's engineers wrote a program that made it run. **Chaos Monkey** picked virtual machines in the production fleet at random and switched them off, during working hours, when the engineers who owned them were at their desks. It ran in production because a test environment has the code but lacks production traffic, data and the real behaviour of downstream services. A service that could not lose a machine without users noticing would be found out on a Tuesday afternoon instead of at three in the morning.

On 21 April 2011 Amazon's largest region, in northern Virginia, had a long outage of its block storage service. Sites that ran there went down for hours, and some went down for days. Netflix ran there too, and kept streaming with higher error rates and no large outage, which its engineers put down in part to having practised losing machines.[^aws] From Netflix's experience comes the rule to **test failure on purpose**. In this lesson, we will examine a failure mode that the first version of Chaos Monkey did not test, where a machine slows down rather than dying outright, which takes down large systems most often.

A service that serves users usually calls several others. Take an API server handling 1,000 requests a second. Half of the requests are "start playback" and call a catalogue service with a latency of 20 ms. The other half are "home page" requests that call the catalogue (20 ms) and then a recommendations service (normally 30 ms), taking 50 ms in all. In the figure below the catalogue is service A and recommendations is service B. Each request holds one of the server's 200 threads for as long as it takes.

By Little's law from lesson 2, threads in use equal the arrival rate multiplied by the time each thread is held. Normally that is 500 req/s × 0.02 s + 500 req/s × 0.05 s = 35 threads out of 200 threads. Now suppose the recommendations service slows to 3 seconds because of a bad deploy, a full disk, a garbage collector pause or a slow dependency of its own. The home page requests now hold a thread for 3.02 s each, requiring 500 req/s × 3.02 s = 1,510 threads out of a pool of 200 threads. The pool fills in under half a second. From then on every request queues for a thread, including the playback requests that never touch recommendations. A service that was merely slow has taken down one that was perfectly healthy.

The cause is one missing configuration parameter. Many client libraries ship with no timeout at all, or with a timeout of a minute, so a call to a slow service waits as long as the service takes.[^default] A **timeout** bounds how long any call may hold a thread. You should set it from the dependency's measured latency (using the percentiles from lesson 9) to a little above its 99.9th percentile, so that healthy calls almost never hit it. The 99.9th percentile is the slowest call in a thousand, so you need many thousands of samples for a stable measurement, which at 500 calls a second takes a few minutes of traffic. If B's 99.9th percentile latency is 250 ms, a timeout of 300 ms fits. You also need to decide what a timed-out call returns. A home page without personal recommendations can show a list of popular titles, because an honest, degraded **fallback** is better than returning an error.

blocks.caption: An API server's thread pool and two services it calls, one of which slows down. We calculate threads in use by Little's law; numbers are illustrative.
blocks.task: Slow B to a second or more, then add guards until every playback request is answered

blocks.text: With B at a latency of 3 seconds and no guards, playback throughput falls to about 13%, because the pool's 200 threads go to whichever requests arrive first, and seven in eight requests time out at the client. If you turn on the timeout alone, playback recovers fully, the home pages go out without recommendations, and the pool runs at 170 of 200 threads. That margin is thinner than it looks, as we will see when we add retries.

A **retry** recovers from a transient fault that will not happen twice, such as a dropped packet, a machine that died mid-call, or a leader election. It does nothing for a persistent fault, such as a service that is slow because it is overloaded, and in that case retrying causes harm. Turn on "Retry ×3" with the timeout in the figure. That setting makes up to three attempts in all (the initial call and two retries), each cut off at 300 ms, with backoff waits of 50 ms and then 100 ms between them. Each home page request now holds its thread for 20 ms + 3 × 300 ms + 150 ms = 1.07 s. The thread pool fills again, playback throughput drops to about a third, and the slow service receives three times as many calls as before. Retrying made the outage worse.
In a chain of services it is worse still. A request at the top passes through several layers, and if each layer retries its own calls, the retries multiply.

blocks.caption: How many calls one request can become, at the bottom of a chain where every call fails.

blocks.text: Three tries at each of five layers produce 3⁵ = 243 calls at the bottom for every one request at the top, and they arrive exactly when the bottom service is already failing. This amplification is a **retry storm**, and it explains why a service that briefly hiccups can stay down after the hiccup is over, as the load from retries alone keeps it overloaded. To prevent retry storms, engineers restrict where and how retries happen. Retry at one layer only, usually the one nearest the user. Cap the number of tries. Give each client a **retry budget** so that it counts its calls and its retries over a recent window, say 10 seconds, and allows a retry only while retries remain under 10% of calls; when most calls fail, the client stops adding retries instead of tripling its load.[^budget] Finally, retry only calls that are safe to repeat, a requirement we will cover in lesson 22.

The delay between retries matters as much as their number. A client that retries immediately, again and again, keeps hitting a server that needs time to recover. **Exponential backoff** doubles the wait after each failure, from 100 ms to 200 ms to 400 ms, up to a cap. Even so, if 100 clients fail at the same moment, they back off by the same durations and retry at the same moments in a synchronised wave each time, and an overloaded server completes fewer requests the larger a wave is.

In March 2015 Marc Brooker of Amazon Web Services published the fix on the AWS Architecture Blog, which is to add **jitter** (randomness) to the wait time. With "full jitter" each client waits a random duration between 0 ms and its current backoff cap, so the 100 clients spread out across the interval instead of arriving together. His simulations showed that full jitter cut both the total number of calls and the time until every client succeeded.

blocks.caption: A hundred clients fail at the same moment and retry. The server handles 20 calls per 100 ms; when sent n calls above that capacity, it completes only 20 × 20 / n calls, so 100 calls at once get 4 calls through. A client that fails waits 100 ms, or with backoff 100 ms doubled at each failure up to 3.2 s. Illustrative numbers.
blocks.task: Compare the three, ending with jitter

blocks.text: Retrying immediately gets every client through in about 3 seconds at the cost of nearly 1,000 calls. Plain exponential backoff sends fewer calls, but the waves stay synchronised and some clients are still failing 8 seconds later. Backoff with jitter finishes in just over 1 second with fewer calls than either alternative. The same synchronisation occurs whenever many machines act on the same schedule, such as caches expiring together (lesson 15), cron jobs starting at midnight, or phones reconnecting after a network blip. You can prevent it by adding random jitter to spread the requests over time.

In his 2007 book *Release It!*, Michael Nygard applied two concepts from traditional engineering to software fault tolerance. A **circuit breaker** wraps calls to one dependency and counts failures. While calls succeed, the breaker remains closed and passes them through. When the failure rate passes a threshold (say 50% of calls over a few seconds, given a minimum volume so that two failures out of three calls do not trip it), the breaker opens, causing every call to fail immediately without waiting and go straight to the fallback. After a pause, say 5 seconds, the breaker enters a half-open state, letting a few calls through to test the dependency, closing if they succeed, and opening again if they fail. In the figure, the breaker opens after 1 second of failures and stays open for 5 seconds. Failing fast frees the caller's threads immediately and removes load from the struggling service so it can recover.[^fuse]

A **bulkhead** is named after the walls that divide a ship's hull into compartments so that a hull breach floods only one compartment. In software it is a separate, bounded thread pool or semaphore for calls to each dependency, here 40 threads for service B. You can size it from normal traffic using Little's law: 500 calls a second × 0.03 s equals 15 threads, so a pool of 40 threads lets B run nearly three times slower before any call to it is rejected. When B slows down, its 40 threads fill and further calls to B are rejected at once, while the other 160 threads keep serving everything else. Netflix packaged timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads and fallbacks into a library called Hystrix and open-sourced it in 2012; every call from its API servers to another service went through Hystrix.

In the figure, using the circuit breaker alone or the bulkhead alone protects playback requests, though the two mechanisms behave differently. The breaker reacts after 1 second of failures and then skips B entirely, recommendations included, until a test call succeeds. The bulkhead never skips B, so the fastest of B's responses still get through, but it keeps 40 threads tied up waiting on B. Production systems use timeouts, a bulkhead and a circuit breaker together.

The last guard protects a service from its own callers. When a server is overloaded, the work it does on a request that will time out anyway is wasted, and the queue it builds increases latency for every request (lesson 2). **Load shedding** rejects excess work early and cheaply, returning a "busy, try later" error in microseconds before reading the request body or touching a database once the queue length or CPU utilisation passes a limit. When ordered by priority, load shedding drops low-priority work such as prefetching and analytics before dropping a user waiting for a video to start. A flawed design that looks similar is a load balancer health check that removes a slow server from rotation; its traffic then shifts to the remaining servers, which overload and slow down in turn until the health check removes every server.[^sps]

Every guard in this lesson is code that executes only when something goes wrong, which is why it so often fails when it is finally needed, whether from a timeout set to the wrong value, a fallback that throws an exception, or a breaker whose threshold is never reached. Netflix built Chaos Monkey to force fault-handling code to run every day. In July 2011 Netflix described a wider suite of fault-injection tools called the Simian Army. Latency Monkey injected artificial delays into calls between services, reproducing the slow-dependency failure from the start of this lesson. Chaos Gorilla simulated the loss of a whole availability zone (one of a cloud region's separate datacentres). Netflix released Chaos Monkey as open source in July 2012.

Netflix later formalised this practice as **chaos engineering**. First, you pick a metric that measures whether the system is healthy from the user's perspective; Netflix used stream starts per second. Next, you state a hypothesis that if a given component fails, that metric will not drop. You then inject the failure in production on a small fraction of traffic first and watch the metric. If it drops, you have found a weakness on your own schedule, with engineers on hand and a way to halt the experiment immediately. In lesson 23, we will see how to keep any single failure, deliberate or not, from reaching every user.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on failing gracefully
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: An API server takes 500 requests a second, each calling a service that normally answers in 20 ms. The service slows to 2 s and the API has no timeout. What happens to the API's threads?
choices: They rise from about 10 threads to about 1,000 threads, so a pool of a few hundred threads fills and even requests that skip that service must wait
They stay at about 10 threads, because each thread waits for the slow call without doing any CPU work of its own
They double, from about 10 threads to about 20 threads, because each request now takes longer while arriving at the same rate as before
items.why: Little's law: threads = rate × time held. 500 × 0.02 = 10; 500 × 2 = 1,000. Once the pool is full, requests queue for threads regardless of what they call.

items.ask: Five layers of services each retry failed calls up to three times. Why can this keep a struggling service at the bottom down?
choices: Retries are sent at a higher priority than first tries, so they push the service's ordinary work to the back of its queue
Each layer's retries multiply the calls to the layer below, up to 3⁵ = 243 calls at the bottom for each request, just when it is failing
Each retry opens a new connection, and the service runs out of sockets long before it runs out of CPU
items.why: Retries at every layer multiply down the call chain. You should retry at one layer, cap the tries, and use a retry budget so a failing service receives less load rather than more.

items.ask: Why add random jitter to exponential backoff?
choices: Clients that failed together otherwise back off by the same amounts and return together, in waves the server cannot serve
Random waits make it harder for an attacker to predict when a client will retry and to block its calls
Jitter shortens each client's waits on average, so a client gets through sooner than it would with plain exponential backoff
items.why: Backoff alone keeps the clients synchronised. Waiting a random duration up to the backoff limit spreads retries across the interval, cutting both total calls and the time until all clients succeed.

items.ask: What does a circuit breaker on calls to a slow dependency do?
choices: It retries each failed call immediately on a different replica of the dependency, until one of them answers
It slows down the caller's whole request rate until the dependency's error rate falls below a threshold
After repeated failures it fails calls at once, returning a fallback, and later lets a few calls through as a test
items.why: Failing fast frees the caller's threads and takes load off the dependency so it can recover. The half-open test determines when normal calls can resume.

items.ask: An API server gives calls to its recommendations service their own pool of 40 threads, apart from its main pool of 200 threads. What does that provide?
choices: Recommendations are answered 40 at a time in parallel, so they come back about 40 times faster
If recommendations get slow, at most 40 threads wait on them and the other 160 threads keep serving everything else
Recommendations can never time out, because they always have threads of their own reserved for them
items.why: A dedicated pool acts as a bulkhead, limiting how much of the caller's capacity one dependency can consume. Calls beyond the 40 threads are rejected at once and use the fallback.

items.ask: A server is overloaded. Which response helps the system recover rather than spreading the trouble?
choices: Let the load balancer's health check remove the slow server, so that its share of traffic goes to the others
Queue every request until it can be served, so that no user's request is ever turned away
Refuse low-priority requests early and cheaply, before doing any work on them, and keep serving the rest
items.why: Load shedding keeps the server doing useful work. Removing a slow server shifts its load onto its neighbours, which then overload as well, while queuing everything increases latency for every request.

items.ask: Why did Netflix run Chaos Monkey in production during working hours?
choices: A test environment lacks production's traffic and real dependencies, and during working hours the engineers who own the service are on hand
Working hours had the most viewers, so a failure then showed its largest effect on stream starts and was easiest to measure against the noise
Machines killed at night came back more slowly, which would have hidden how fast recovery could be
items.why: Failure-handling code runs only when something fails, and only production has the real traffic and dependencies to test it. Triggering failures during business hours exposes weak spots when engineers are at their desks instead of at 3 a.m. Viewing peaks in the evening, not during working hours.

summary: **A slow dependency is worse than a dead one.** Because threads in use equal arrival rate multiplied by holding time, a call that slows from 30 ms to 3 s can exhaust a thread pool and block unrelated requests.
**Every call needs a timeout and a fallback.** Set the timeout just above the dependency's 99.9th percentile latency, and return a degraded fallback response when it fires.
**Retries help with transient faults and hurt during overload.** Retry at one layer only, cap the number of attempts, and enforce a retry budget.
**Retries multiply down a chain.** Three tries at each of five layers can generate 243 calls at the bottom for a single user request.
**Back off with jitter.** Exponential backoff spreads retries over time, while random jitter prevents clients that failed together from retrying in synchronised waves.
**A circuit breaker fails fast.** After failure rates cross a threshold, it skips the dependency for a cooldown period and then tests it with a few calls, giving both services room to recover.
**A bulkhead caps the resources one dependency can consume.** A separate, bounded thread pool keeps a slow service from exhausting threads needed by other endpoints.
**Shed load early and by priority.** Rejecting excess requests cheaply is better than queuing work that will time out, and better than pulling slow servers out of load-balancer rotation.
**Test failure on purpose.** Chaos Monkey and its successors forced fault-handling code to run every day in production while engineers were at their desks.

migration.title: Seven years to move
migration.text: Netflix's account of the move, published when it finished in January 2016, says the 2008 corruption was the reason, and that it chose to rebuild its services for the cloud rather than move the old ones over as they were.

aws.title: The April 2011 outage
aws.text: A network change in one availability zone left many of Amazon's Elastic Block Store volumes trying to re-mirror themselves at once, and the storage control plane jammed. Netflix kept its stateless services off EBS volumes and ran across multiple availability zones, so losing one zone caused little disruption.

default.title: Defaults that wait for ever
default.text: Java's standard HttpURLConnection, for instance, has default connect and read timeouts of 0 ms, which means no limit. A call to a server that accepts the connection and never answers holds its thread until the process is restarted.

budget.title: Retry budgets
budget.text: A budget tracks the ratio of retries to initial requests over a recent time window, and a client stops retrying when the budget is spent. Google's SRE book recommends capping retries at 10% of total requests per client, alongside a maximum of three attempts per request.

fuse.title: From the fuse box
fuse.text: An electrical circuit breaker trips when current is too high so a fault in one appliance does not set the building's wiring on fire, and a person must flip it back once the fault is fixed. The software version resets itself automatically via half-open test calls so engineers do not have to be paged to reset it.

sps.title: Stream starts per second
sps.text: Netflix chose stream starts per second as its primary health metric because it directly reflects user experience: when playback breaks, users press play and nothing happens, causing the rate to drop within seconds. Its daily and weekly traffic curve is predictable enough that an unexpected dip stands out immediately.
